items.text: We introduce a new language representation model called BERT, which stands for Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers.
items.why: Introduces BERT model name and full expansion.
items.plain: We introduce BERT, which stands for Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers.

items.text: Unlike recent language representation models (Peters et al., 2018a; Radford et al., 2018), BERT is designed to pretrain deep bidirectional representations from unlabeled text by jointly conditioning on both left and right context in all layers.
items.why: Defines core architectural novelty: deep bidirectional pre-training across all layers.
items.plain: Unlike earlier language models, BERT pre-trains deep bidirectional representations from unlabeled text by conditioning jointly on both left and right context in all layers.

items.text: BERT alleviates the previously mentioned unidirectionality constraint by using a “masked language model” (MLM) pre-training objective, inspired by the Cloze task (Taylor, 1953).
items.why: Introduces the Masked Language Model objective to achieve bidirectionality.
items.plain: BERT overcomes unidirectionality by using a masked language model pre-training objective inspired by the Cloze task.

items.text: The masked language model randomly masks some of the tokens from the input, and the objective is to predict the original vocabulary id of the masked
items.why: Explains how the Masked Language Model objective operates.
items.plain: The masked language model hides random input tokens so the model must predict their original vocabulary IDs.

items.text: Unlike left-toright language model pre-training, the MLM objective enables the representation to fuse the left and the right context, which allows us to pretrain a deep bidirectional Transformer.
items.why: Explains why Masked LM enables deep bidirectional representations.
items.plain: The masked language model objective combines left and right context, allowing pre-training of a deep bidirectional Transformer.

items.text: In addition to the masked language model, we also use a “next sentence prediction” task that jointly pretrains text-pair representations.
items.why: Introduces the second pre-training task: next sentence prediction.
items.plain: We also use a next sentence prediction task to jointly pre-train text-pair representations.

items.text: There are two steps in our framework: pre-training and ﬁne-tuning.
items.why: Outlines the two main operational phases: pre-training and fine-tuning.
items.plain: Our framework consists of two steps: pre-training and fine-tuning.

items.text: During pre-training, the model is trained on unlabeled data over different pre-training tasks.
items.why: Describes what happens during the pre-training step.
items.plain: During pre-training, the model trains on unlabeled data across different pre-training tasks.

items.text: For ﬁnetuning, the BERT model is ﬁrst initialized with the pre-trained parameters, and all of the parameters are ﬁne-tuned using labeled data from the downstream tasks.
items.why: Describes what happens during the fine-tuning step.
items.plain: For fine-tuning, the model is initialized with pre-trained parameters and all parameters are updated using labeled task data.

items.text: Model Architecture BERT’s model architecture is a multi-layer bidirectional Transformer encoder based on the original implementation described in Vaswani et al. (2017) and released in the tensor2tensor library.1 Because the use of Transformers has become common and our implementation is almost identical to the original, we will omit an exhaustive background description of the model architecture and refer readers to Vaswani et al. (2017) as well as excellent guides such as “The Annotated Transformer.”2
items.why: Identifies the core architecture as a multi-layer bidirectional Transformer encoder.
items.plain: BERT uses a multi-layer bidirectional Transformer encoder architecture.

items.text: We primarily report results on two model sizes: BERTBASE (L=12, H=768, A=12, Total Parameters=110M) and BERTLARGE (L=24, H=1024, A=16, Total Parameters=340M).
items.why: Gives exact architectural parameters and size of BERT-Base and BERT-Large.
items.plain: BERT-Base uses L=12, H=768, A=12 (110M total parameters) and BERT-Large uses L=24, H=1024, A=16 (340M total parameters).

items.text: Input/Output Representations To make BERT handle a variety of down-stream tasks, our input representation is able to unambiguously represent both a single sentence and a pair of sentences (e.g., ⟨Question, Answer ⟩) in one token sequence.
items.why: Explains unified input representation for single sentences and sentence pairs.
items.plain: Our input representation handles both single sentences and sentence pairs in a single token sequence.

items.text: The ﬁrst token of every sequence is always a special classiﬁcation token ([CLS]).
items.why: Defines the mandatory classification token [CLS].
items.plain: The first token of every sequence is always a special classification token, [CLS].

items.text: The ﬁnal hidden state corresponding to this token is used as the aggregate sequence representation for classiﬁcation tasks.
items.why: Explains how [CLS] token vector is used in task classification.
items.plain: The final hidden state of the [CLS] token serves as the combined sequence representation for classification.

items.text: First, we separate them with a special token ([SEP]).
items.why: Explains the separator token [SEP] for sentence pairs.
items.plain: We separate sentence pairs using a special token, [SEP].

items.text: Second, we add a learned embedding to every token indicating whether it belongs to sentence A or sentence B. As shown in Figure 1, we denote input embedding as E, the ﬁnal hidden vector of the special [CLS] token as C ∈RH, and the ﬁnal hidden vector for the ith input token as Ti ∈RH.
items.why: Defines segment embeddings and mathematical notation for final states.
items.plain: We add a learned segment embedding indicating sentence A or B, noting the input embedding as E, the [CLS] hidden vector as C, and token hidden vectors as Ti.

items.text: For a given token, its input representation is constructed by summing the corresponding token, segment, and position embeddings.
items.why: Defines exact summation construction of total input embeddings.
items.plain: A token's input representation is constructed by adding together its token, segment, and position embeddings.

items.text: In order to train a deep bidirectional representation, we simply mask some percentage of the input tokens at random, and then predict those masked tokens.
items.why: Details the random masking strategy of the Masked LM.
items.plain: To build a deep bidirectional representation, we randomly mask a percentage of input tokens and predict them.

items.text: In all of our experiments, we mask 15% of all WordPiece tokens in each sequence at random.
items.why: States the precise masking percentage used in experiments.
items.plain: In all experiments, we randomly mask 15% of WordPiece tokens in each sequence.

items.text: The training data generator chooses 15% of the token positions at random for prediction.
items.why: States the sampling scheme for prediction positions.
items.plain: The training data generator randomly selects 15% of token positions to be predicted.

items.text: If the i-th token is chosen, we replace the i-th token with (1) the [MASK] token 80% of the time (2) a random token 10% of the time (3) the unchanged i-th token 10% of the time.
items.why: Gives exact 80/10/10 probability breakdown for masked token substitution.
items.plain: Chosen target tokens are replaced with [MASK] 80% of the time, a random token 10% of the time, and left unchanged 10% of the time.

items.text: In order to train a model that understands sentence relationships, we pre-train for a binarized next sentence prediction task that can be trivially generated from any monolingual corpus.
items.why: Describes the binary Next Sentence Prediction task construction.
items.plain: We pre-train a binary next sentence prediction task where candidate sentence pairs are easily generated from monolingual text.

items.text: Speciﬁcally, when choosing the sentences A and B for each pretraining example, 50% of the time B is the actual next sentence that follows A (labeled as IsNext), and 50% of the time it is a random sentence from the corpus (labeled as NotNext).
items.why: Gives exact 50/50 proportion for true vs random next sentences.
items.plain: 50% of the time sentence B is the actual next sentence (IsNext), and 50% of the time it is a random sentence (NotNext).

items.text: As we show in Figure 1, C is used for next sentence prediction (NSP).5 Despite its simplicity, we demonstrate in Section 5.1 that pre-training towards this task is very beneﬁcial to both QA and NLI.
items.why: Links vector C to NSP task prediction.
items.plain: The vector C is used to predict whether sentence B follows sentence A.

items.text: The input embeddings are the sum of the token embeddings, the segmentation embeddings and the position embeddings.
items.why: Reiterates input embedding composition formula.
items.plain: Input embeddings are formed by summing token embeddings, segmentation embeddings, and position embeddings.

items.text: For the pre-training corpus we use the BooksCorpus (800M words) (Zhu et al., 2015) and English Wikipedia (2,500M words).
items.why: Lists corpora and word counts used for pre-training.
items.plain: We pre-train on BooksCorpus (800 million words) and English Wikipedia (2,500 million words).

items.text: BERT instead uses the self-attention mechanism to unify these two stages, as encoding a concatenated text pair with self-attention effectively includes bidirectional cross attention between two sentences.
items.why: Explains how self-attention achieves bidirectional cross attention in fine-tuning.
items.plain: BERT processes concatenated text pairs with self-attention, naturally integrating bidirectional cross attention between sentences.

items.text: For each task, we simply plug in the taskspeciﬁc inputs and outputs into BERT and ﬁnetune all the parameters end-to-end.
items.why: Describes parameter updates during task-specific fine-tuning.
items.plain: We attach task-specific inputs and outputs to BERT and fine-tune all parameters end-to-end.

items.text: At the output, the token representations are fed into an output layer for tokenlevel tasks, such as sequence tagging or question answering, and the [CLS] representation is fed into an output layer for classiﬁcation, such as entailment or sentiment analysis.
items.why: Explains output mappings for token-level vs sequence-level tasks.
items.plain: Token hidden states feed into output layers for token tasks, while the [CLS] representation feeds into output layers for sequence classification.

items.text: To ﬁne-tune on GLUE, we represent the input sequence (for single sentence or sentence pairs) as described in Section 3, and use the ﬁnal hidden vector C ∈RH corresponding to the ﬁrst input token ([CLS]) as the aggregate representation.
items.why: Describes fine-tuning input and aggregate output state for GLUE.
items.plain: For GLUE tasks, input sequences use BERT representations, and vector C from the [CLS] token serves as the aggregate representation.

items.text: The only new parameters introduced during ﬁne-tuning are classiﬁcation layer weights W ∈ RK×H, where K is the number of labels.
items.why: Defines parameters added for GLUE classification tasks.
items.plain: Fine-tuning adds only a single matrix of classification weights W of shape K by H, where K is the number of target labels.

items.text: Both BERTBASE and BERTLARGE outperform all systems on all tasks by a substantial margin, obtaining 4.5% and 7.0% respective average accuracy improvement over the prior state of the art.
items.why: Reports overall accuracy improvement of BERT variants over prior state-of-the-art on GLUE.
items.plain: BERT-Base and BERT-Large outperform all baseline systems across all GLUE tasks, improving average accuracy by 4.5% and 7.0% over prior best results.

items.text: As shown in Figure 1, in the question answering task, we represent the input question and passage as a single packed sequence, with the question using the A embedding and the passage using the B embedding.
items.why: Explains input formatting for SQuAD question-passage pairs.
items.plain: For question answering, question and passage are packed into a single sequence using segment embedding A for the question and B for the passage.

items.text: We only introduce a start vector S ∈RH and an end vector E ∈RH during ﬁne-tuning.
items.why: Defines task-specific vectors introduced for SQuAD.
items.plain: During fine-tuning, we only add a start vector S and an end vector E.

items.text: The probability of word i being the start of the answer span is computed as a dot product between Ti and S followed by a softmax over all of the words in the paragraph: Pi = eS·Ti P
items.why: Gives exact probability formula for answer start position in SQuAD.
items.plain: The probability of word i being the start of the answer is the dot product of Ti and S, softmaxed over all words.

items.text: The score of a candidate span from position i to position j is deﬁned as S·Ti + E·Tj, and the maximum scoring span where j ≥i is used as a prediction.
items.why: Defines candidate answer span scoring formula.
items.plain: A candidate answer span from position i to j is scored as S·Ti + E·Tj, selecting the highest-scoring span where j >= i.

items.text: Our best performing system outperforms the top leaderboard system by +1.5 F1 in ensembling and +1.3 F1 as a single system.
items.why: Reports SQuAD v1.1 F1 improvements over top leaderboard systems.
items.plain: Our best system outperforms the top leaderboard entry by +1.5 F1 in ensemble mode and +1.3 F1 as a single model.

items.text: We treat questions that do not have an answer as having an answer span with start and end at the [CLS] token.
items.why: Explains modeling strategy for unanswerable questions in SQuAD v2.0.
items.plain: Unanswerable questions are treated as having an answer span that starts and ends at the [CLS] token.

items.text: For prediction, we compare the score of the no-answer span: snull = S·C + E·C to the score of the best non-null span
items.why: Gives null answer score formula for SQuAD v2.0.
items.plain: The no-answer score snull is computed as S·C + E·C.

items.text: We predict a non-null answer when ˆ si,j > snull + τ, where the threshold τ is selected on the dev set to maximize F1.
items.why: Defines decision rule for predicting answer vs no-answer in SQuAD 2.0.
items.plain: We predict a non-null answer when its best span score exceeds snull + τ, tuning threshold τ on development data.

items.text: We observe a +5.1 F1 improvement over the previous best system.
items.why: Reports F1 performance gain on SQuAD v2.0.
items.plain: BERT achieves a +5.1 F1 improvement over the previous best system on SQuAD v2.0.

items.text: When ﬁne-tuning on the SWAG dataset, we construct four input sequences, each containing the concatenation of the given sentence (sentence A) and a possible continuation (sentence B).
items.why: Explains input sequence construction for SWAG task choices.
items.plain: For SWAG fine-tuning, we create four input sequences pairing the context sentence with each candidate continuation.

items.text: The only task-speciﬁc parameters introduced is a vector whose dot product with the [CLS] token representation C denotes a score for each choice which is normalized with a softmax layer.
items.why: Describes added parameters and scoring mechanism for SWAG.
items.plain: We add a single vector whose dot product with C gives a choice score, which is normalized with softmax.

items.text: BERTLARGE outperforms the authors’ baseline ESIM+ELMo system by +27.1% and OpenAI GPT by 8.3%.
items.why: Reports accuracy improvements of BERT-Large on SWAG benchmark.
items.plain: BERT-Large beats the baseline ESIM+ELMo system by +27.1% and OpenAI GPT by 8.3% on SWAG.

items.text: No NSP: A bidirectional model which is trained using the “masked LM” (MLM) but without the “next sentence prediction” (NSP) task.
items.why: Defines 'No NSP' ablation model variant.
items.plain: 'No NSP' is a bidirectional model trained with masked LM but without next sentence prediction.

items.text: LTR & No NSP: A left-context-only model which is trained using a standard Left-to-Right (LTR) LM, rather than an MLM.
items.why: Defines 'LTR & No NSP' ablation model variant.
items.plain: 'LTR & No NSP' is a left-only model trained with standard left-to-right language modeling without NSP.

items.text: In Table 5, we show that removing NSP hurts performance signiﬁcantly on QNLI, MNLI, and SQuAD 1.1.
items.why: Demonstrates empirical impact of removing NSP task.
items.plain: Removing next sentence prediction significantly degrades model performance on QNLI, MNLI, and SQuAD 1.1.

items.text: The LTR model performs worse than the MLM model on all tasks, with large drops on MRPC and SQuAD.
items.why: Demonstrates empirical impact of left-to-right constraint vs bidirectional MLM.
items.plain: The left-to-right model performs worse than the masked language model on all tasks, with large drops on MRPC and SQuAD.

items.text: We can see that larger models lead to a strict accuracy improvement across all four datasets, even for MRPC which only has 3,600 labeled training examples, and is substantially different from the pre-training tasks.
items.why: Shows that scaling model size strictly improves accuracy even on tiny datasets.
items.plain: Larger models yield strict accuracy gains across all evaluated datasets, including MRPC which has only 3,600 training samples.

items.text: However, we believe that this is the ﬁrst work to demonstrate convincingly that scaling to extreme model sizes also leads to large improvements on very small scale tasks, provided that the model has been sufﬁciently pre-trained.
items.why: Highlights key finding that extreme pre-trained scaling aids small downstream tasks.
items.plain: This work demonstrates that scaling pre-trained models to extreme sizes produces substantial gains even on small-scale downstream tasks.

items.text: To ablate the ﬁne-tuning approach, we apply the feature-based approach by extracting the activations from one or more layers without ﬁne-tuning any parameters of BERT.
items.why: Describes experimental setup for evaluating BERT in a feature-based setup.
items.plain: To test a feature-based approach, layer activations are extracted without fine-tuning BERT's parameters.

items.text: These contextual embeddings are used as input to a randomly initialized two-layer 768-dimensional BiLSTM before the classiﬁcation layer.
items.why: Explains architecture attached on top of fixed BERT features for NER.
items.plain: Extracted contextual embeddings are passed into a randomly initialized two-layer 768-dimensional BiLSTM before classification.

items.text: The best performing method concatenates the token representations from the top four hidden layers of the pre-trained Transformer, which is only 0.3 F1 behind ﬁne-tuning the entire model.
items.why: Reports feature-based performance relative to full model fine-tuning.
items.plain: Concatenating token representations from the top four hidden layers scores within 0.3 F1 of fine-tuning the complete model.

items.text: This demonstrates that BERT is effective for both ﬁnetuning and feature-based approaches.
items.why: Concludes that BERT works effectively for both fine-tuning and feature-based setups.
items.plain: This shows that BERT is effective for both fine-tuning and feature-based applications.

items.text: • 80% of the time: Replace the word with the [MASK] token, e.g., my dog is hairy →
items.why: Defines the main component of the masked token substitution procedure.
items.plain: 80% of the time, the target word is replaced with the [MASK] token.

items.text: • 10% of the time: Replace the word with a random word, e.g., my dog is hairy →my
items.why: Defines the random token replacement rule in masking.
items.plain: 10% of the time, the target word is replaced with a random word.

items.text: • 10% of the time: Keep the word unchanged, e.g., my dog is hairy →my dog
items.why: Defines the unchanged token rule in masking.
items.plain: 10% of the time, the target word is kept unchanged.

items.text: The advantage of this procedure is that the Transformer encoder does not know which words it will be asked to predict or which have been replaced by random words, so it is forced to keep a distributional contextual representation of every input token.
items.why: Explains why the randomized masking procedure forces contextual representations.
items.plain: Because the Transformer encoder cannot predict which words need to be guessed or were replaced randomly, it must keep contextual representations for every input word.

items.text: Among the three, only BERT representations are jointly conditioned on both left and right context in all layers.
items.why: Highlights BERT's core architectural distinction of joint bidirectional conditioning across all layers.
items.plain: Among BERT, OpenAI GPT, and ELMo, only BERT representations use both left and right context together in every layer.

items.text: 50% of the time B is the actual next sentence that follows A and 50% of the time it is a random sentence, which is done for the “next sentence prediction” task.
items.why: Explains how sentence pairs are sampled for Next Sentence Prediction.
items.plain: Half of the time, sentence B actually follows sentence A, and the other half it is a random sentence from the dataset.

items.text: The LM masking is applied after WordPiece tokenization with a uniform masking rate of 15%, and no special consideration given to partial word pieces.
items.why: Specifies WordPiece tokenization and the overall 15% masking rate.
items.plain: Masking happens after breaking words into WordPiece tokens at a 15% rate, without treating sub-words differently.

items.text: We train with batch size of 256 sequences (256 sequences * 512 tokens = 128,000 tokens/batch) for 1,000,000 steps, which is approximately 40
items.why: Details the pre-training batch size, steps, and dataset iterations.
items.plain: The model is pre-trained with a batch size of 256 sequences (128,000 tokens per batch) for 1,000,000 steps, totaling about 40 passes over the 3.3 billion word dataset.

items.text: We use Adam with learning rate of 1e-4, β1 = 0.9, β2 = 0.999, L2 weight decay of 0.01, learning rate warmup over the ﬁrst 10,000 steps, and linear decay of the learning rate.
items.why: Specifies the exact optimizer and learning rate schedule for pre-training.
items.plain: Training uses the Adam optimizer with a learning rate of 1e-4, β1 = 0.9, β2 = 0.999, L2 weight decay of 0.01, a linear warmup over 10,000 steps, and linear learning rate decay.

items.text: The training loss is the sum of the mean masked LM likelihood and the mean next sentence prediction likelihood.
items.why: Defines the total pre-training loss objective.
items.plain: The training loss combines the average masked language model likelihood and the average next sentence prediction likelihood.

items.text: To speed up pretraing in our experiments, we pre-train the model with sequence length of 128 for 90% of the steps.
items.why: Details the two-stage sequence length optimization used during pre-training.
items.plain: To save pre-training time, the model uses a sequence length of 128 for 90% of the training steps.

items.text: Then, we train the rest 10% of the steps of sequence of 512 to learn the positional embeddings.
items.why: Explains how full sequence lengths are introduced to train positional embeddings.
items.plain: The remaining 10% of training steps use a sequence length of 512 to learn positional embeddings.

items.text: • GPT uses a sentence separator ([SEP]) and classiﬁer token ([CLS]) which are only introduced at ﬁne-tuning time; BERT learns [SEP], [CLS] and sentence A/B embeddings during pre-training.
items.why: Contrasts BERT's pre-training token/embedding structure with OpenAI GPT.
items.plain: GPT adds sentence separators ([SEP]) and classifier tokens ([CLS]) only when fine-tuning, whereas BERT learns [SEP], [CLS], and sentence A/B embeddings during pre-training.

items.text: Our task-speciﬁc models are formed by incorporating BERT with one additional output layer, so a minimal number of parameters need to be learned from scratch.
items.why: Describes how task-specific downstream models are constructed during fine-tuning.
items.plain: Downstream models add a single output layer to BERT, so only a tiny fraction of parameters are trained from scratch.

items.text: Answer: Yes, BERTBASE achieves almost 1.0% additional accuracy on MNLI when trained on 1M steps compared to 500k steps.
items.why: Provides empirical evidence on the necessity of 1,000,000 pre-training steps.
items.plain: BERTBASE gains nearly 1.0% higher accuracy on MNLI when pre-trained for 1M steps instead of 500k steps.

items.text: However, in terms of absolute accuracy the MLM model begins to outperform the LTR model almost immediately.
items.why: Demonstrates that MLM outperforms Left-to-Right models despite slower convergence.
items.plain: In terms of actual accuracy, the masked language model surpasses the left-to-right model almost immediately.
